October 29, 2026

Via Federal e-rulemaking portal



Debbie-Anne A. Reese
Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street NE, Room 1A
Washington, DC, 20426


RE: DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC; Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for
Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions To Intervene, and Competing Applications (91 FR
56879)

Dear Secretary Reese and Deputy Secretary Clay,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the preliminary permit application for the DeepGreen
Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project No. 15423-000.

Oceana is concerned about the thermal effects on the surrounding waters; marine mammal harms via
increased vessel traffic, disturbance to food sources, and acoustic impacts; fishery disruptions; and
negative impacts on Alaska's coastal economy. Due to these risks, the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (FERC) must reject DeepGreen Cook Inlet's Project No. 15423-000.



    I. UNDERWATER DATA CENTERS MAY DIRECTLY HARM MARINE MAMMALS
       AND FISHERIES

Because this novel industry has yet to be implemented at scale and studied, there is limited information
available on direct impacts of constructing underwater data centers. However, an understanding of the
impacts of ocean industrialization is sufficient to predict likely adverse consequences for marine
ecosystems and coastal communities.

    A. Impacts to the Cook Inlet beluga whale and other marine mammals

The proposed activities could increase risks to the Cook Inlet beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas) and
other marine mammals in the area. This population is listed as endangered under the Endangered
Species Act (ESA) and depleted under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA). Only an estimated
331 individuals remain, down from historic estimates near 1,300.1 Other endangered and threatened

marine mammals in the area include the Western distinct population segment (DPS) of the Steller sea
lion (Eumetopias jubatus) and seasonal visits from the Western North Pacific DPS of the humpback
whales (Megaptera novaeangliae).2

Critical habitat

The majority of the upper Cook Inlet, nearshore areas in the southwestern part of the inlet, and
Kachemak Bay are designated as Cook Inlet beluga whale critical habitat under the ESA.3 Critical
habitat is defined as “specific areas within the geographical area occupied by the species, at the time it is
listed . . . , on which are found those physical or biological features (I) essential to conservation of the
species and (II) which may require special management considerations or protection.”4 The Cook Inlet
beluga uses this area for calving, feeding, and protection from predators.5

Increased underwater noise
Ocean noise pollution is of special concern for whales and other cetaceans, as they are highly dependent
on sound as their principal sense and largely utilize acoustic cues for navigation, communication,
foraging, and predator avoidance.6

On land, data centers generate significant noise pollution, with internal noise levels reaching up to 96 A-
weighted decibels (dBA), above the 85 dBA threshold considered harmful to human hearing.7 Noise
emitting from the outside of data centers varies depending on size and but is estimated between 40 to 70
dBA.8 Because sound travels more than four times faster and over much greater distances in seawater
than in air, underwater noise generated by underwater data centers has the potential to affect marine
species across broad areas of the ocean.9 Increased ambient noise may increase stress, disrupt

     B. Fishery impacts

Pacific Salmon population overlap

This project overlaps with important habitat for all five species of Pacific salmon. Pacific salmon are
anadromous fish, meaning that they spawn in fresh water, migrate to the ocean to forage and mature, and
return to fresh water to spawn and begin the cycle again.10 These fish are sensitive to thermal stress -
negatively impacting health, decreasing spawning success, and in extreme conditions, even leading to
mass mortality events.11 The thermal output of underwater data centers in this area has the potential to
disrupt these important migratory patterns, impacting spawning patterns and generations of salmon to
come.
"Forever chemicals"

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as “forever chemicals,” are found in various
parts of data centers including cooling systems, semiconductors, and hardware, due to their durability
and heat resistance.12 When constructing data centers underwater, it is likely that these chemicals will be
released into the surrounding water. Certain PFAS compounds have high bioaccumulation rates in fish,
meaning that they can be stored in the tissues of fish and may have an increased concentration in
predatory fish at higher trophic levels.13 This could translate to a higher level of PFAS in fish that
recreational and commercial anglers catch in the surrounding waters.

     II. UNDERWATER DATA CENTERS MAY NEGATIVELY IMPACT ALASKA’S
         COASTAL ECONOMY

Alaska's coastal economy and cultural heritage are directly tied to the oceans. The oceans are
economically important for recreation and tourism, commercial and recreational fishing, ship and boat
building, marine transportation, and more. In Alaska alone, the coastal economy provides nearly 46,000
jobs and yields $11.2 billion in GDP annually.14 Salmon are also an important species to the culture of
Alaska. Three out of four Alaskans reported feeling strongly connected to salmon, according to a survey
by The Salmon Project.15 They are also an important part of commercial, sport, and subsistence fishing,
as well as vital to key ocean food webs.

By introducing industrial infrastructure into Alaska's coastal waters, underwater data centers could
threaten the state’s economic engine if there is impact on navigable waters, fisheries, or perceived
disruption to the pristine environment that underpins the state's seasonal tourism economy.


                                                 CONCLUSION

The absence of studies on underwater data centers should not be mistaken for an absence of risk. We
urge FERC to reject the preliminary permit to build DeepGreen Cook Inlet's Project No. 15423-000.



Sincerely,



Julia Singer

Defense Campaign Manager

Oceana
